Trying to Conceive

Anxiety, depression and emotional support during fertility treatment

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Fertility treatment can involve hope, disappointment and a difficult sense of helplessness. You may follow every instruction and still face an uncertain result. Support should help you cope with that uncertainty, protect your relationships and look after your mental health. It should never imply that being anxious, depressed or insufficiently positive is the reason treatment has not worked.

Why treatment can feel so emotionally demanding

Appointments, medication timings, tests and waiting for results can take over a large part of everyday life. A person may work hard to eat well, attend every visit and follow a treatment plan, yet still be unable to control the outcome. That mismatch between effort and result can be exhausting.

Intimate examinations and repeated discussions of reproductive health can also feel exposing. Feeling uncomfortable does not mean that you are uncooperative or ungrateful for care. You can ask what an examination involves, who will be present and how to pause or discuss a concern.

Some people feel grief, anger, fear, shame or numbness; others move between these feelings. Partners may react differently to the same news. There is no single emotional response that proves someone is coping properly.

Accurate information can make decisions more manageable, but knowledge and effort cannot guarantee a pregnancy. Emotional support is valuable throughout assessment, treatment, a pause or a decision to stop, whatever the eventual outcome.

What infertility means and when to seek assessment

Infertility is commonly defined as not achieving pregnancy after twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse. That definition is a starting point for clinical assessment, not a judgment about a person’s value or a requirement that everyone wait a year before asking for help.

Assessment is generally recommended sooner when the person providing eggs is aged thirty-five or older: commonly after six months, with more immediate discussion over forty. Irregular or absent periods, a known reproductive condition, previous cancer treatment or another clear concern can justify earlier advice.

People using donor sperm or other assisted routes to parenthood need advice suited to their circumstances. The timing of assessment and treatment should not be reduced to a universal rule about a year of intercourse or insemination.

A diagnosis may provide an explanation and treatment options, but it does not promise that every available treatment will succeed. A clinician should explain the likely benefits, limits and alternatives in a way that supports an informed decision.

There can be more than one medical contributor

Fertility difficulties can involve sperm production or function, ovulation, the fallopian tubes or other parts of the reproductive system. Sometimes more than one factor is present, and sometimes routine testing does not identify a clear cause.

Examples of possible male contributors include a varicocele, previous genital infection, testicular injury and other medical or reproductive conditions. Immune-related mechanisms may be considered in selected circumstances, but a general mention of immunity is not a reason for everyone to have specialised immune tests or treatment.

Where relevant, assessment of both partners can prevent the entire burden of investigation being placed on one person. A finding in one partner is medical information for planning care, not evidence of fault, failure or an obligation to disclose private details to relatives.

Treatment choices depend on the findings and the people involved. The psychological effects deserve attention even when a cause is identified or there is a clear clinical plan.

Stress deserves care without becoming another source of blame

Infertility and its treatment can be stressful. That is different from proving that ordinary worry causes infertility or that a person’s distress caused an unsuccessful cycle. Those claims can add guilt to an already difficult experience.

The HFEA states that there is no conclusive evidence that higher stress reduces the chance of having a baby through fertility treatment. ASRM’s patient information similarly distinguishes improving wellbeing from guaranteeing pregnancy through stress reduction.

Anxiety or depression can still need treatment in their own right. Difficulty sleeping, concentrating, working or maintaining relationships matters even if it has no established effect on a fertility outcome. Support should aim to reduce suffering, not make calmness another condition you must meet to deserve success.

Do not abruptly stop prescribed mental-health medication because you are trying to conceive. Discuss treatment with the relevant clinicians so they can consider your health, pregnancy plans and any fertility medicines together.

Family questions, stigma and social pressure

Repeated questions about when a baby is coming, what treatment has been tried or whose fertility is the problem can feel intrusive. Comments that suggest a person is defective or has failed at an expected role can be especially painful.

Some people encounter rejection, exclusion or an absence of practical and emotional support. Others find gatherings centred on pregnancies and children difficult, particularly when people respond with pity, boastfulness or unwanted comparisons.

The burden can fall disproportionately on women, including when a male factor has been identified. WHO recognises that infertility can be associated with stigma, anxiety, depression and, in some settings, violence. These pressures are not confined to one country and should not be excused as an unavoidable part of family life.

You can choose what to share and with whom. A brief response such as “We are keeping treatment details private, and we will share news when we want to” may be enough. A trusted person can also help communicate boundaries so you do not have to repeat them.

It is reasonable to skip a particular celebration, limit fertility conversations or leave an upsetting discussion. Boundaries can preserve supportive relationships rather than requiring complete withdrawal from everyone.

Work, money and a sense of identity

Fertility care can affect work schedules, energy, finances and plans for the future. Repeated appointments or uncertainty about the next cycle may make ordinary commitments harder to organise. These practical demands can add to emotional strain.

Where possible, ask the clinic for a clear account of expected appointments, costs and whom to contact when plans change. Decide carefully what information you want to share at work and whether a trusted person can help with transport, meals or other tasks.

A lack of financial help can make care harder to access, but support should not be measured only by money. Listening, respecting privacy and offering a specific practical task can matter greatly. Equally, no one should use financial assistance to control treatment decisions.

If stigma or exclusion starts to narrow your life, consider discussing it with a counsellor or support group. You do not have to wait until you feel completely overwhelmed to seek that support.

1. Put some attention on choices you can control

It is natural to wonder whether this cycle will work or how long treatment will take. Those questions may have no certain answer. Alongside them, identify a few decisions that remain yours: whom to contact, what to ask at the next appointment, and how to organise one manageable part of the week.

Choose goals that are not a test of fertility success. Finishing a work task, making space for a hobby or asking for help with an appointment can provide a sense of agency without claiming control over conception.

A brief list of questions or a simple plan can reduce the mental work of remembering everything. If tracking becomes another pressure, simplify it. There is no requirement to optimise every meal, activity or thought.

Some people find journaling, relaxation or gentle activity useful. Choose what helps you and check any treatment-related activity restrictions with the clinic. The aim is a more manageable day, not proof that you are doing enough to become pregnant.

2. Make room for honest conversations

If you have a partner, try to name the feeling as well as the practical problem. Saying that you feel frightened, disappointed or out of control may be more useful than assuming the other person already understands.

Choose a time when neither person has to rush into work or another commitment. A planned check-in can create room for listening. You might ask whether the other person wants to talk, be listened to or work through a decision together.

Different coping styles do not necessarily mean unequal commitment. One person may want information while the other needs a break from the topic. Agreeing on some times to discuss treatment and some times to rest from it can help both needs be heard.

The same principle applies to a friend, relative or other trusted support person if you are pursuing treatment without a partner. Your clinic can also explain unexpected results and next steps; you should not have to resolve every medical uncertainty within a personal relationship.

3. Keep some time for ordinary enjoyment

Treatment can become the subject of every conversation. A walk, a shared meal, time with a friend or a familiar hobby can create a small space in which life has another focus. It does not have to be an expensive trip or an ambitious plan.

You can tell a friend that you would appreciate company without discussing fertility that day. On another day, talking may be exactly what helps. The important point is having some choice rather than performing optimism for other people.

Enjoyment is not a duty, and a difficult day does not cancel progress. If travel or physical activity is planned during treatment, check whether appointments, medicines or recovery needs affect what is practical.

Persistent loss of interest in everything you usually enjoy is also a reason to seek mental-health support. A suggestion to have fun should not be used to dismiss depression.

4. Protect closeness without making sex another obligation

When sex becomes scheduled around conception or treatment, it may start to feel like a task. Affection, companionship and time together can help a relationship retain meaning beyond treatment, but neither partner owes sexual activity to prove commitment.

Closeness can include a hug, holding hands, a conversation or simply sharing an activity. If both people want sexual contact, discuss comfort and preferences without turning novelty or frequency into another performance target.

Pain, fatigue, low desire or treatment instructions may change what feels possible. Ask the clinic about any temporary restrictions and seek advice for persistent pain or distress. Do not push through unwanted or uncomfortable activity because it is described as good for the relationship.

A qualified counsellor can help with different needs, resentment or communication difficulties. Support can be individual or shared; it should respect privacy, consent and each person’s boundaries.

5. Allow your identity to remain bigger than treatment

A fertility diagnosis describes a medical situation. It does not erase the other parts of who you are: a friend, partner, professional, creative person, community member or someone with interests and values unrelated to parenthood.

It can help to keep one connection or activity that is not organised around treatment. This is not a demand to minimise how much having a child matters. It is permission for other parts of life to matter too.

Continuing treatment, taking a break or stopping can each involve complex feelings. These choices should be explored with accurate information and appropriate support, not framed as evidence that someone has tried hard enough or given up.

There is no promise that treatment will resolve every difficulty or lead to a child. Your worth and entitlement to care do not depend on that outcome.

How friends and family can offer useful support

Begin by asking what would help and listening to the answer. Some people want to discuss appointments; others prefer practical help or a conversation about something else. Do not assume that being willing to listen gives you permission to ask for private medical details.

Avoid predicting success, assigning blame or explaining the situation as deserved fate. Comparisons with someone who became pregnant after relaxing can leave the person feeling responsible for an outcome they cannot control.

Comments about enjoying child-free freedom, being lucky to have fewer responsibilities or inevitably becoming a parent can minimise grief. A more useful response acknowledges that the situation is hard and that you are available without promising a solution.

Offer something concrete if appropriate, such as a lift, a meal or company after an appointment. Respect a declined invitation or a request for privacy. Do not circulate treatment updates or suggest another intervention unless the person welcomes that discussion.

Support can continue after an unsuccessful cycle or a decision to stop. The need to be heard does not end when there is no new treatment plan to discuss.

When professional or urgent support is needed

A fertility counsellor, psychologist or other qualified mental-health professional can help with grief, decision-making, anxiety, depression and relationship strain. Ask the clinic what is available, whether there is a cost, and whether individual or group support would suit you.

Seek help if distress is persistent, daily functioning is becoming difficult, you are withdrawing from relationships, or sleep, appetite, concentration or substance use is changing in a concerning way. You do not need to wait for a crisis or a formal diagnosis to ask.

Threats, coercion or violence from a partner or family member are not problems you must solve by becoming pregnant or communicating more effectively. Seek confidential support from a local domestic-abuse service or healthcare professional, using a safe way to contact them.

If you feel at immediate risk of harming yourself, cannot keep yourself safe or are in immediate danger from someone else, contact local emergency services or an urgent crisis service. If it is safe, ask a trusted person to stay with you while you get help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fertility organisations recognise the emotional burden of infertility and recommend access to counselling and support. Stress-reduction approaches are intended to improve wellbeing; they do not guarantee treatment success.

WHO identifies stigma and unequal social burdens as important effects of infertility. Clinical assessment and psychological care should address individual circumstances without blaming either partner or treating a fertility outcome as a measure of personal worth.

How BeMama can help

Keep a short note of questions, the next appointment and one kind of support you would welcome. Let any tracking serve you; it should not become a score for how well you are coping.

When to seek help

Persistent anxiety, depression, pain or relationship distress deserves professional support. Discuss prescribed medicines with your clinicians rather than stopping them yourself. For immediate danger or an inability to stay safe, use local emergency or crisis support.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Following treatment carefully cannot guarantee its outcome.
  • Distress is not evidence that you caused infertility or an unsuccessful cycle.
  • Small choices, honest conversations and ordinary enjoyment can support wellbeing.
  • Closeness should respect consent and treatment-related needs.
  • Family support should protect privacy and avoid predictions or blame.
  • Professional support is appropriate before distress becomes a crisis.

Frequently asked questions

Did my anxiety cause fertility treatment to fail?

You should not assume that it did. There is no conclusive evidence that higher stress reduces the chance of having a baby through fertility treatment. Your distress still deserves care.

Will relaxing improve my chances of pregnancy?

Stress reduction can improve wellbeing, but it does not guarantee pregnancy. Advice to relax should not replace medical assessment or add blame.

Do I always need to wait a year before seeking fertility advice?

No. Age, known conditions and treatment history can justify earlier assessment. Around age thirty-five and above, evaluation is commonly considered after six months, and sooner in some circumstances.

What can I say when relatives keep asking for news?

You can say that you are keeping treatment private and will share updates when you choose. You do not owe anyone test results or an explanation of whose fertility is involved.

Is it wrong to avoid a baby shower or family event?

No. You can set limits around situations that feel painful. Consider keeping other supportive connections so a boundary does not turn into unwanted isolation.

What if my partner and I cope differently?

Different reactions are common. A planned conversation about what each person needs can help; counselling is also available when communication or decisions feel difficult.

Do we need to keep having sex to protect the relationship?

No one owes sex as a relationship duty. Closeness can take many forms, and sexual activity should be wanted, comfortable and consistent with medical advice.

Should I stop antidepressants while trying to conceive?

Do not stop prescribed medicines abruptly. Ask your mental-health and fertility clinicians to review the benefits, risks and appropriate plan together.

When should I ask for counselling?

At any point you would find it useful, especially if distress, isolation, relationship strain or changes in daily functioning persist. You do not need to wait for a crisis.

How can a friend help after an unsuccessful cycle?

Listen without predicting success or proposing an immediate fix. Offer specific practical help, respect privacy and continue support even if treatment pauses or stops.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
